Large earthquakes always have fore-shocks and aftershocks. We never know which of the earthquakes is the 'big one' until the tension is released and things go back to normal. The fact of the matter is that these earthquakes are happening in one of the most tectonically active places on the planet.

edit: I completely missed the second part of what you were saying. The tension is released by earthquakes, but more earthquakes will happen. Where this is happening plays a lot into this and it is really interesting. In the middle of the Pacific Ocean there is a spreading ridge, which is basically where magma is welling up and creating new crust. On either side of the Pacific you have this same crust subducting and sinking under the continental plates. Continental plates are made of a lighter type of rock than ocean plates (continental have more silicone and feldspar, while ocean plates are rich in iron and magnesium). The new ocean crust is more buoyant than the old ocean crust because it is warmer as well. The weight of the old ocean crust sinking into the mantle is pulling on the new ocean crust, causing it to spread apart, exposing more magma, which cools and creates more ocean crust. Basically this creates an ocean sized convection cell in the mantle, and the crust is riding along the top of that. Japan is the part of the continental crust that is overriding the ocean crust (the reason there is ocean on both sides of Japan is because the Sea of Japan is basically a crumple zone (if you want to know more, google back arc basin). The simplified model of this process that is taught in most intro geology courses would have one large earthquake, and then things stop moving. The real world is not that easy though. At this scale there is no such thing as a strait line, because you can't fit a strait line on a globe. This means that there are cracks that will have to run 90° to any linear feature to get it to fit on a sphere. Its the same reason we have trouble making accurate world maps that are useful. Take into account that we are dealing with rock, which almost never breaks in strait lines (many minerals do, but pure minerals are rare compared to rock), and you have zones where tension is released by an earthquake, only to be stored in another area close by.
